issues.legal_issue: A disciplinary tribunal may inquire into a disproportionate-assets allegation as misconduct when the rule governing referral covers matters involving misconduct generally.
material_facts: A disproportionate-assets allegation was referred to the disciplinary proceedings tribunal after a rule had come into force permitting referral of matters involving misconduct by gazetted and non-gazetted officers.
The tribunal found the officer guilty of the disproportionate-assets charge, and the disciplinary authority acted on its report.
issues.conclusion: The disciplinary proceedings tribunal had jurisdiction to inquire into the disproportionate-assets charge; the fact that the allegation also fell under a criminal law and described graver misconduct did not remove it from the tribunal’s jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Act, 1960, as amended by Andhra Pradesh Act 6 of 1993, provided that the Government may refer cases to the tribunal. Rule 3, as amended by G.O.Ms. No. 514 dated 15 October 1994 and in force when this case was referred, permitted referral of matters involving misconduct. Disproportionate assets constitute misconduct under Rule 2(b) of the relevant disciplinary rules and the applicable Conduct Rules. The Court also relied on Article 309 in rejecting the contention that the officer could be proceeded against only outside the disciplinary rules. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.

predicates.disciplinary_referral_proceeding: The Government referred an employee’s alleged misconduct to a disciplinary proceedings tribunal for inquiry and report.
predicates.referral_rule_covers_misconduct_generall: The rule governing the referral permits the tribunal to inquire into matters involving misconduct generally.
predicates.disproportionate_assets_alleged: The employee was alleged to possess assets disproportionate to the employee’s known sources of income.

issues.definition: When a general misconduct referral rule applies to a disciplinary referral concerning alleged disproportionate assets, the tribunal has jurisdiction to inquire into that misconduct.

issues.legal_issue: An employee’s failure to comply with the applicable notice or reporting requirement for acquiring property may constitute misconduct, and the requirement of prior intimation is not a requirement to obtain prior permission.
material_facts: The charge alleged that the officer acquired immovable and movable assets without prior permission.
The Court found that the officer had neither given prior intimation to the Government about the immovable-property acquisitions nor reported the relevant transactions as required.
The disciplinary tribunal found that the officer had not provided the required information or intimation, and the Court considered the charge in light of its supporting allegations.
issues.conclusion: The officer violated the applicable property-acquisition requirements and was guilty of misconduct; the distinction between prior intimation and prior permission did not defeat the charge on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 9(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964 requires previous intimation to the Government before an employee acquires or disposes of immovable property. Rule 9(2) requires an employee to report forthwith a transaction concerning movable property exceeding the specified value; its proviso requires previous sanction for a transaction conducted otherwise than through a regular or reputed dealer. The Court distinguished intimation, which apprises the Government, from permission, which requires positive approval, and held that failure to give the required intimation or report breached the rule. Such a breach constituted misconduct under Rule 2(b) of the applicable disciplinary rules. No earlier cases were relied on for this issue.

rule.if: disciplinary_proceeding and government_employee_acquired_property and failed_required_property_reporting and charge_particulars_support_reporting_breach

predicates.disciplinary_proceeding: An employee’s conduct was considered in a disciplinary proceeding.
predicates.government_employee_acquired_property: A government employee acquired property covered by the applicable property-reporting requirements.
predicates.failed_required_property_reporting: The employee did not provide the notice, intimation, report, or sanction required for the relevant property transaction.
predicates.charge_particulars_support_reporting_bre: The allegations supporting the charge described facts that, if established, amounted to failure to meet the applicable property-reporting requirement.

issues.definition: If an employee acquires covered property in a disciplinary case and fails a reporting requirement described by the charge, that breach is misconduct.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing tribunal may not reweigh evidence or substitute its factual conclusion for a disciplinary finding supported by relevant legal evidence, unless the finding is perverse or unsupported by legal evidence.
material_facts: The disciplinary tribunal examined witnesses and documentary exhibits and found the officer guilty of both charges.
The disciplinary authority accepted the tribunal’s findings and removed the officer from service.
The Supreme Court found that the disciplinary findings rested on legally permissible substantive evidence and that the reviewing tribunal had interfered with those findings.
issues.conclusion: The reviewing tribunal could not sit as an appellate authority, reconsider the evidence to decide the correctness of the charges, or substitute a different finding where relevant legal evidence reasonably supported the disciplinary decision.
issues.legal_principle: Judicial review of disciplinary proceedings concerns the manner in which the decision was made and does not extend to a fresh examination of the evidence to determine the correctness of the charges. Where relevant material accepted by the disciplinary authority reasonably supports its conclusion, a reviewing tribunal may not reweigh that material, substitute its own finding, or interfere with punishment on that basis. A perverse finding unsupported by legal evidence may, however, be treated as a legal flaw and quashed. No earlier cases were identified or relied on in the judgment for this principle.

predicates.judicial_review_of_disciplinary_decision: A court or tribunal is reviewing a disciplinary decision rather than hearing an appeal on the merits of the employee’s conduct.
predicates.findings_supported_by_relevant_legal_evi: Relevant evidence that the disciplinary authority accepted reasonably supports the disciplinary findings.
predicates.findings_perverse_or_without_legal_evide: The disciplinary findings are irrational or lack legal evidentiary support.

issues.definition: When disciplinary findings have reasonable support in relevant legal evidence and are not perverse or unsupported, judicial review does not permit the reviewing tribunal to reweigh the evidence or replace those findings with its own.
